sentences.text: Pterodaustro is a genus of ctenochasmatid pterodactyloid pterosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 105 million years ago.
This creature possessed a uniquely elongated tail with twenty-two caudal vertebrae, a feature more extensive than that of any other pterodactyloid.
The skull was very elongated, reaching up to 29 centimeters in length, featuring a long, narrow head and a curved beak.
Its modified teeth were arranged in two long grooves along the jaw edges rather than in separate sockets, measuring 3 centimeters long with a width of only 0.2 to 0.3 millimeters.
Research confirmed that these bristle-like structures were true teeth containing enamel, dentine, and pulp.
Adult Pterodaustro reached a maximum wingspan of approximately 3 meters and a body mass of approximately 9.2 kilograms.
Pterodaustro is frequently nicknamed the "flamingo pterosaur" due to its diet potentially giving it a pink hue, similar to modern flamingos.
It is one of the best-known pterosaurs because fossils exist representing all growth stages, from egg to adult.
Pterodaustro was the first pterosaur found in the Southern Hemisphere.
The genus Pterodaustro was named in 1969 by José Bonaparte, with the first valid description of the genus published in 1970, establishing the type species Pterodaustro guiñazui.
Pterodaustro was discovered in 1970 by paleontologists José Bonaparte and José Román Guiñazú in the Lagarcito Formation in San Luis, Argentina.
Over 750 specimens of Pterodaustro have been collected from the Loma del Pterodaustro site, with 288 catalogued by 2008.
A site containing many fossils of this flying reptile was found in northern Chile by Kevin Pdian and Michael Bell.
Researchers suggest that the formation containing Pterodaustro fossils originated from successive, sudden floods that destroyed the nests of this reptile.

Pterodaustro likely used its tooth comb for filter feeding, a method similar to that of modern flamingos, supported by the abundance of small, hard-shelled aquatic crustaceans in the fossil site sediment.
Gizzard stones have been found in the stomachs of Pterodaustro specimens, marking the first report of such structures in any pterosaur.
Juvenile Pterodaustro grew rapidly in their first two years, reaching about half of adult size.
Biomechanical modeling suggests Pterodaustro juveniles could fly, contradicting hypotheses that they could only glide early and fly late.
A Pterodaustro embryo preserved in an egg was reported in 2004.
Medullary bone tissue was reported in a Pterodaustro femur in 2009, potentially making it the first reported occurrence of such tissue in a non-dinosaurian reptile.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Pterodaustro may have been nocturnal, though this hypothesis has been questioned by some researchers.
Pterodaustro likely required frantic, low-angled take-offs in open areas, similar to modern geese and swans.
José Bonaparte initially assigned Pterodaustro to the family Pterodactylidae in 1970 and later to Pterodaustriidae in 1971.
Cladistic studies from 1996 placed Pterodaustro within the family Ctenochasmatidae alongside other filter feeders.
A 2018 study placed Pterodaustro within the tribe Pterodaustrini of the family Ctenochasmatidae, in a basal position relative to Beipiaopterus and Gegepterus.
Pterodaustro belongs to the parent group Lophocratia and is classified in the class Reptilia.
Pterodaustro lived from the Aptian to the Albian stages, between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago.
In 2021, researchers suggested that the medullary bone tissue found in Pterodaustro might actually be crushed endosteal tissue.
